Question: Can the mutual fund SIP industry prevent the market from crashing?
Answer: There isn't any mutual fund SIP industry. What exists is a stock market regulation body like SEBI in India. In India the SEBI puts restrictions on how much a stock can rise or fall. While SEBI lays down the foundation, the stock exchanges implement the policy. To curb undesirable volatility, all exchanges are required to fix uniformly the daily price band at 10% and a weekly overall limit of 25%. However in case of scrips up to the value of Rs. 20, the price bands could be decided by the stock exchanges. The price band would be calculated on the basis of the closing price of the scrip on the previous day, which will be the weighted average price of the last half hour of trading in the scrip on that exchange. This is how SEBI attempts to prevent a market steep accent or avalanche. But it can protect a daily fall only. When the market opens the next day, the stocks may move the same way.

Question: Is physical gold a wise investment or real estate?
Answer: Neither is a good investment if I may say so. Gold has returned 14% YoY since 2018. It has returned nearly 11% from 2008, ever since I have been keeping track. Note that this is pre-tax. This is quite a good return but hold your horses for a moment. You are talking of physical gold and investment. What is investment typically? It is something that gives periodic return like interest or dividend and when liquidated generates capital gain. The gain should be substantial. People look at absolute returns but that is very misleading. The true return is measured by CAGR (for interest paying instruments) or XIRR (for market linked instruments). Gold is of the latter category. Physical gold is a dead investment as it doesn’t generate periodic dividend. One gets attached to the yellow metal and doesn't sell it. And if this is jewellery for the wife, forget selling at all. So all that rise in value is on paper. Yes, technically it can always be sold, but it rarely ever happens. Hence it is a dead investment. Now coming to real estate, more or less the same is true. So, property is also a dead investment. If you look at the XIRR on property considering all input costs, all the AMCk, property taxes paid, periodic maintenance, etc., etc., this is about 8.5% to 12% before taxes. If Gold is what attracts you, consider SGBs instead.

Question: My UK student visa was refused because I can't explain my modules properly. If I apply again, how many chances does the embassy have to take my interview again?
Answer: I am the unhappy bearer of the news. You think that your UK Student Visa was refused because you could not explain the modules properly. This is your supposition. You must ask yourself - why was this question even asked to you? I can tell you that over 50% of the students seeking a Visa (other than to the USA) are not even called for an Interview. If the background grades are good, the previous college/university is reputed, there are sufficient funds, etc., the interview is waived off. Once a person (student) is called for an interview, it means that some aspects of the application are not clear. The consulate officer wants to make sure and clear all doubts. Even before the interview, the consular officer has already made up his mind to reject (75%). Unless the application is too bad, the officer wants to be fair. So the person is called for the interview. At this time, all sorts of questions are asked - what is the career objective, where will you study, what will you study, what are your subjects, how do these subjects align with your career objective, etc? If you apply again, there is a good chance that your application will be denied (if the previous application was very recent) and almost near certainty that you will be called for an interview again if the application was not rejected outright. For the USA also, the in-person presence can be a mere formality if the visa-seeker is talented, has good marks (GRE/ToEFL scores), seeking admission to a reputed university, has funds, etc.

Question: What are the top strategies for budgeting and managing monthly expenses?
Answer: I often quote Yes, Minister in my answer. In this book/TV Series, Sir Arnold Robinson is the Cabinet Secretary, the de-facto head of the British Civil Service. He and Sir Humphrey (Permanent Secretary to the (fictional) Department of Administrative Affairs or DAA) are once lecturing Bernard Wooley, the Principal Private Secretary to the Minister of DAA: Bernard, When people don’t know what you are doing, they don’t know what you are doing wrong. This very apt, witty and profound statement applies to all facets of life. Leave aside the humour and satire but think. You are spending and you do not know how to save. You are unable to save, Of course, you don’t and can’t. You simply don’t know what you are doing and therefore you don’t know what you are doing wrong. The solution is simple and one should ideally do it in Excel. Stage 1: You must document. You must document your expenses each and every one of them down to the smallest fraction. You spend some money in tea/coffee, it may be very little but you must write it down. You went to buy vegetables, write that down. You paid a small sum for parking whilst you were at the supermarket? Write it down. You buy that expensive phone - write it down in the book. Nothing must be lost or missed out. Your daily expense book must begin with “Beginning bal b/f”, all expenses, all cash withdrawals, and your ending balance at the end of the day. This must tally with your real wallet. Stage 2: Categorize. Categorize your expenses into 6–10 categories - no more. Even 10 are perhaps too many. Make these as - Rent or Mortgage, Travel, Food & Groceries, Eating Out/Restaurant, Mobile & Internet, Leisure & Entertainment, Shopping, and Miscellaneous. The last (Miscellaneous) is tricky - try not to dump a lot into this. Stage 3: Create a Pivot Table. Create a pivot table on a new sheet based on Month (X-axis) vs Category (Y-axis) or vice-versa. (Please don’t ask me how to do this - this is something you should learn and do.) The Pivot table will tell you where your money is going. Stage 4: Analyse. Analyse the Pivot Table. See the high-ticket items. You will be surprised to discover that many small items like Tea/Coffee at a restaurant can significantly add up. So decide where you can cut down. Stage 5: Implement the Plan. (This is self-explanatory).

Answer: To present a good background on how good the idea of an ID card will be in the UK and how popular it is in Europe, I present you a transcript of a very popular British sitcom/satire on the Political System in the UK Yes Minister, Series 1, Episode 5 - The Writing on the Wall Sir Humphrey (Permanent Secretary to the Department of Administrative Affairs): Well, there's no doubt about it, the writing's on the wall. Bernard Wooley (Principal Private Secretary to the Minister of DAA): The public should think kindly towards the Administration, because of the Europass. Sir Humphrey: Quite. Jim Hacker, the minister: Europass? Sir Humphrey: European Identity Card. (addressing Bernard) Bernard, Surely you've informed the Minister? (to the Minister): Didn't you do your boxes? Jim Hacker: No, I was redrafting the re-draft of the draft. Sir Humphrey: Well, Brussels is about to decree that there is to be a new European Identity Card to be carried by all citizens of the EEC. Jim Hacker: Good idea? Frank (Jim's political advisor): Good idea? Jim Hacker: Good idea? Sir Humphrey: Not a good idea? Jim Hacker: Political suicide! Trying to make British people carry Identification Papers? They'll call it a Police State. Is this what we fought two world wars for? Sir Humphrey: Well, minister ... It's little more than a sort of driving licence. Jim Hacker: It's the last nail in my coffin. Bernard Wooley: You might get away with calling it "Euroclub Express". Jim Hacker (upset and angry) Bernard, either shut up or get out! Frank: Can't the Foreign Office introduce it? Sir Humphrey: That was the Prime Minister's suggestion, but the Foreign Secretary said it was a Home Office matter, and for the Home Office, it was essentially an administrative matter, and the PM agreed. Frank: Pass the parcel. Jim: Can you blame them when you can hear it ticking? Sir Humphrey: The identity card bill is planned to be the last action of this Department. Wonderful ammunition for the anti-Europeans. Jim: Doesn't the Foreign Office realise the damage to the European idea? Sir Humphrey: That's why they support it. Jim: The Foreign Office is pro-Europe, isn't it? Sir Humphrey: Yes and no... if you'll forgive the expression. The Foreign Office is pro-Europe because it is really anti-Europe. The Civil Service was united in its desire to make sure that the Common Market didn't work. That's why we went into it. Jim: What are you talking about? Sir Humphrey: Minister, Britain has had the same foreign policy objective for at least the last 500 years: To create a disunited Europe. We have fought with the Dutch against the Spanish (defeat of the Spanish Armada), with the Germans against the French (Napoleonic Wars) and with the French against the Germans and the Italians (WW-II). Divide and rule, you see. Why should we change now, when it's worked so well? Jim: That's all ancient history surely? Sir Humphrey: Yes, and current policy. We had to break the whole thing up, so we had to get inside. We tried from the outside, but it wouldn't work (a reference to the European FTA). Now, we can make a complete pig's breakfast of the whole thing. Set the Germans against the French, the Italians against the Dutch... The Foreign Office is terribly pleased, it's just like old times. Jim: But we're all committed to the European ideal. Sir Humphrey: (chucking) Really, Minister! Jim: Why are we then pressing for an increase in the membership? Sir Humphrey: For the same reason. It's just like the United Nations. The more members it has, the more arguments it can stir up, the more futile and impotent it becomes. Jim: What appalling cynicism. Sir Humphrey: Yes. We call it diplomacy, Minister. Frank: How will the other countries feel about identity papers? Won't they resist too? Sir Humphrey: No. No. The Germans will love it, the French will ignore it, and the Italians and the Irish will be too chaotic to enforce it. Only the British will resent it. Question: Is our principal amount safe in mutual funds?
Answer: No. Unfortunately, your principal investment is not safe when invested in shares (direct equity) or equity-based mutual funds (indirect equity). For that matter, the principal amount is not secure even in debt-based mutual funds. But here is the catch. The principal amount is not safe even with bank deposits. This is because of tax and inflation. Let me clarify before you shout at me with indignation: Today (Aug-24), the bank FD rates vary between 7% to 7.8% - SBI gives 6.8% (I have even seen a hoarding announcing fixed deposit at 9% by a coop bank. But I am not too sure about the liquidity of such banks). Anyway, let me assume a rate of 7% as given by sound banks such as SBI, HDFC, ICICI, etc. (Rates may vary and you may arrive at your own calculations). Next, we must consider the inflation factor. The current inflation rate is officially < 4%. But is is really so? The practical picture tells me that is is more like 6.5%. Finally, the income tax rate. Now tax rate is as per slab. Cutting the complexities, let me further assume the final tax rate is 20%. So the equation is like this: a) Deposit of ₹1,00,00 at 7% b) After 1 year, the interest is ₹7,000 c) After tax, it will reduce to ₹5,600. Hence the person has ₹1,05,600 at the end of year 1. d) The net effect of 6.5% inflating is that this money value had eroded to ₹98,736. e) There you go. You have already lost ₹1,264 off the principal. Then there is another factor. At this time, the bank deposit rates are very high. I don't expect them to stay there. The industry is crying at the high rate of borrowing and sooner or later, the RBI will bring down the REPO rate. When that happens, the banks will reduce deposit rates also. So what about Mutual Funds? Good fund schemes return 12~13% on an average year-over-year. This is not interest but an estimated annuity return. It is not guaranteed but it is a reasonable expectation. Equity funds are taxed differently. But without considering the ₹1.25 lakh LTCG exemption per year, and applying the same calculation, the value of ₹1 L in MF is equivalent to ₹1,05,187.50 at the end of Y1 (assuming a 12.5% return and inflation of 6.5%). I explained how/why/when the bank FD rates may fall but the MF returns are linked to the market and have been constantly rising. If the stock market crashes tomorrow, the investment can become zero also. This is often the fear in the minds of the ordinary people. The question is - how likely will this happen? We cannot predict. I have seen major falls and deep corrections in 1997 (SE Asia currency crisis), 2001 (dot-com bust), 2008 (sub-prime lending crisis) and a brief busy in 2020 (COVID crisis). In 2005, the BSE Sensex was around 4500. Today it is near 79,000. That is a rise of over 16.26% YoY. Question: Which mutual fund is high expenses ratio in 2024?
Answer: Please don't fret too much on MF expense ratio. There are many people and theories who say - invest in funds with low expense ratio. They do not understand perfectly. While it is true that funds that have lower expense ratio will return more, there are other factors too. For example, a Direct Plan has lower expense ratio than a Regular Plan. This is because the fund pays out commission to agents which they don’t have to in Direct Plan. So the Direct Plan’s NAV is higher, return is higher, etc. But also consider this: Now I know that I am oversimplifying here but let me know which company will you choose to invest in? Costs constitute the middle line. Lower cost does mean higher profit. But this is as far as it goes. If the top line (revenue) is low, no matter the middle line (costs), the bottom line (return/profit) will be lower also. I have seen many posts and comments say that invest in Index funds (a passive fund type) because their expense ratio is minimal and therefore they return more than other funds (aka Actively managed funds). I silently shake my head, chuckle and say “tch, tch”. This is not only misleading but just as much untrue. I have been investing since 2008. Earlier I was investing without research, based on tips and recommendations, etc. From 2015, I have been doing extensive research and then actively managing the portfolio myself. My portfolio today is 55% Equity Funds and 45% Debt-oriented Hybrid funds. Now for hard truth and personal experience. Index returns (NIFTY/SENSEX) from 2015 are around 17%. Index funds linked to NIFTY-50, SENSEX-30, BSE-100, etc., will typically return same as the benchmark. Passively managed index funds have a typical expense ratio of 0.15% to 0.25%. This is so low because there is a small team managing the fund. There is hardly anything to mange as the fund mimics the baseline index by stocks and % holding. This is what an index fund will return whatever be the expense ratio. But my portfolio which was 65:35 in favour of equity (till 2020) and now 55:45 in favour of equity is returning me over 20%. I have an investment in UTI NIFY-50 Direct Plan but that is less than 2% of the total portfolio. (I stopped SIP in this plan long ago.) In 2020, my returns were near 23%. This is in spite of the fact that my portfolio is balanced beaten equity and debt and my funds have typically an expense ratio of 1% to 2%. I have beaten the index and in turn the index funds comfortably. Why is that? This is because expense ratio is not everything. Expense ratio is internal cost of the fund AMC. What we get as a return is after the costs. Not convinced? Bandhan Core Equity Fund - Regular Plan has an expense ratio of 1.85% but its 3-year return is 25.15%. This is more than most index funds (almost all). The Direct Plan has an expense ratio of 0.67% and the 3-year returns are 26.6%. So again saying … Don’t let the expense ratio raise your BP and hypertension. Is this what you are doing - overthinking? Then please stop. An investor should look at the annuity returns - short-term up to 2 years and long-term from 3 years to 10 years. They should look at the trends. They should look at the CRISIL rating. Many website will provide you an SIP planning and projection. I have it also in my Retirement Planning spreadsheet (check it out in my space’s “About” page. Invest in top quality funds by doing research. People who do not wish to do a research, do not wish to monitor the growth/loss, those who are too much bothered about taking corrective steps, talk about and advocate index funds. I am NOT saying that index funds are bad. All I am saying is that there are better options. More than investing blindly, create and follow a plan, for a purpose, measurable, time bound, relevant and achievable (S.M.A.R.T. goal or plan). I never look at expense ratio and I do think that I have done well. There is a very ill-informed comment here: Everyone who succeeds to beat index will credit it to their “skill”. Everyone who fails to beat index will credit it to their “bad luck”. Over 60% of the funds underperform … … and then there is a tirade. Essentially, I am being told that I am boasting; my evidence is anecdotal, etc. My answer is - Yes and No. Yes. I did my research and that is why I am seeing the benefit. Let me ask anyone, don’t you inspect the goods before buying? Don’t you go to the supermarket or local greengrocer and check out the stuff? If you don’t and then the vegetables are rotten or the meat is smelly, will you say that you were unlucky and 60% (or whatever stuff) sold in the market is bad/underperforming? Question: I am working as a consultant and my company sends me the salaries of other employees every month. I send it to them as soon as it is credited. Is it taxable?

All these come under the expense head “Salaries Paid/Payable”. These are directly deductible in your company’s I&E statement. Your Salary No different than any other employee’s salary. Same treatment. Your share of profit if any is added to your salary income under income from business. You will be liable to pay personal income tax as per slabs. So you will be paying tax for your company and your personal income. Hope this makes it clear.

Question: Do you feel that the senior citizens in India are being unjustly taxed on their income, which is passive in nature? Did their preferential treatment in the old tax regime have no merits?
Answer: The Government has been trying to reduce public debt. PPF, NSC, KVP and such Small Savings Schemes (SSS) are public debt. The government will have to pay this money back to the depositors, at one time or another. The government does not want to increase this debt further. Next, when people invest in various forms of 80C instruments, they reduce tax. The government wants to collect more tax. It is unable to expand the tax net - to include small traders, cash-only businesses, farmers, etc. Businessmen can reduce their net tax by charging many of the expenses to their businesses. Just as an example, Mukesh Ambani can buy a Maybach on one of his Reliance shell companies accounts, use it for personal purposes and change the running/maintenance to the business. Not only that, he can claim 33% depreciation. This means that in 3 years, he can buy a brand-new car. Whereas, a humble salaried class must buy a 2-wheeler on loan and pay for everything plus interest from own pocket. How fair is that? The point is the government cannot increase the number of people paying taxes honourably or out of political compulsions. Those left are the salaried class. They cannot hide. So they face the “bullets”. Hence the government has introduced the New Tax Regime. These many schemes in Section 10, Section 24, Section 80, etc., exist in India and similar countries. These schemes were introduced to promote saving and at the same time let people save on tax. The tax rebates were the incentive. These rebates/exclusions are available in the Old Tax Regime only. But the old tax regime is not very good either. There are huge gaps in income slabs and tax rates. Most people earning up to ₹15 lakhs pay lesser tax under the new tax regime. May I add that in other countries there are no rebates for house rent paid, interest paid on education or home loans, savings schemes for taxes, health insurance premiums, leave travel assistance, etc. The New Tax Regime may have been introduced recently (by the Modi Government) but the background research work has been going on since the days of P Chidambaram as the FM. (People credit MMS/PVNR for economic reforms but these were imposed by the IMF and previous FM Yashwant Sinha of the 4-month Chandrashekhar government had prepared the final draft.) You are specifically asking about Senior Citizens. That point did not escape me. I am a senior citizen myself. Regular citizens or Senior citizens - anyone with regular income by way of salary/pension, bank interest, SSS interest, income via Mutual Funds, etc. cannot escape tax. This is immaterial of Old or New Tax Regime. In fact, senior citizens should not use 80C. One is blocking up to ₹1,50,000 for a tax rebate of up to ₹30,000 + Cess. Senior citizens are not expected to be paying home or education loans. They cannot claim HR exemption or LTA as they do not earn a salary. So there is no attraction for the old tax regime. They should switch to the New Tax Regime. I too switched recently.

Question: I made a payment to my friend through phone pay as a loan but now the person passed away after 2 days. How can I get my money back through law?
Answer: If you give someone money by any traceable method (bank transfer, UPI, cheque, etc.), that it is just a proof that you indeed paid that money to that someone. This does not prove that it was a loan. Even if you mention “LOAN” in the UPI transfer, it is your personal reference. For any third person, it could be interpreted that YOU OWED the money and repaid back. The only way to prove a loan is a notarised agreement on a non-Judicial stamp paper (₹100 is good enough usually but ₹500 stamp paper is better). The agreement must mention names of lender (party of the first part), and borrower (party of the second part). Then the document/agreement must mention the amount, repayment terms, whether there shall be any interest, etc. The agreement should be signed by both, witnessed by at least one third person and then notarised. This proves an irrefutable claim. (If such a document is made, the borrower can and should insist on signed receipts when payment is made in part or full. I understand that no one does this, no one goes to that much trouble, showing that much distrust between good friends, relations, etc. But if the amount is large, then this is very advisable. What defines “large” is for you to decide. You must also be aware of the other person whether s/he is reliable or not. Friendships and money does not gel well together. You asked what you should do now in your above situation. You can only appeal to the good faith and sense of the next of kin of your dead friend. You can only hope that he will repay you back. Generally good people do that. I am guessing that you paid your friend who was sick and hospitalised. He needed urgent money for treatment. But unfortunately he passed away. If this is the case, it will be insensitive of you to demand repayment in the hour of crisis. You can/should wait. You also mentioned “through law”. I am afraid that without a firm document, you have no legal recourse. This also indicates that maybe the heirs of your friend are not inclined to repay. If that is the case, my advice is to seek legal counsel. I am not a lawyer or expert in these matters. I am just telling what I think is the case for you. Question: Is TDS a scam? One who is entitled to a refund, does he get interest on the amount that the government has held for some time?
Answer: Let us discuss just the salaried class where TDS is most applicable. I will not get into the tax slabs, etc. I will simply assume that the net taxable income is ₹15 lakhs and on this 30% tax + cess is applicable. I will further assume Old Tax Regime is being used. But that is while filing returns and computing the tax real time. The balance tax refundable is actual tax paid via TDS less net tax payable by computation. But what is TDS practically. It is the income tax deducted by the employer while paying the monthly salary. This is how they do it: a) Annual projected income = (sum of gross salary paid from 1-Apr till last month) + (gross salary of this month * remaining months this FY) b) Consider tax exemptions and other declaration provided by the employee c) Calculate project tax for the year using the old tax regime. d) Subtract the TDS till last month. Get the tax payable till EOY. e) TDS amount for this month = (d) / number of months left in the year including this one In January, the employers ask the proof of investments for (b). The TDS for Jan-Feb-Mar is calculated on the basis of actual proof. This is where excess TDS may happen because employee does not provide proof or investment is less than projected as in (b). The TDS is sometimes slightly more because employers round up the tax deductible to the next higher rupee. On the whole, I have found that if one is meticulous and procedural, there is hardly any excess TDS. I have rarely ever received a refund. In fact, during my working life, I usually owed a tax. (On the other hand in the UK and USA, the employers deduct excess tax so that they are not penalised for deducting less; there I have usually received a refund.) Now coming to the point of interest payable on excess tax paid/refund owed: All these complexities and issues go away if one files by the new tax regime. Wait for a couple of years or more and the Old Tax Regime will be history. No more HRA exemption, no more deduction of interest paid on education and home loan, no more 80C/80D rebates, etc. Just standard deductions and then spread out tax slabs will apply. This is how it works in other countries.

Question: Is it worth taking a 60 lakh rupees loan and studying a master’s in civil engineering in the UK?
Answer: I believe that you are from India (reference to “lakhs”). Please take this very earnest advice from me - don't do this. It will be a very foolish step. I fully concur with the answer given by Gopalkrishna Vishwanath Sir. I will add more to that from personal experience. (BTW, ₹60 lakhs is a lot of money for a Masters in Civil Engineering. Which college are you planning to attend?) My son went to the UK in Jan-2021 (missed Sep because of COVID). He attended and completed his Masters in Adv Engineering Design from Brunel Univ London, Uxbridge. The total cost for the year was £28,000 including fees. He secured distinction. All of us were very happy and thought that his path is now bright. Then we applied for his 2-year Graduate Study Visa (cost = ~ £3000). This enabled him to work for 2 years while he found a work sponsor. However, he didn't get any offers for nearly 13 months. We must have applied to at least 300 companies during that period. All employers wanted people with local experience, having a valid UK Driving license, unwilling to sponsor work permit, etc. Finally, when we were just about to give up, he received an offer. He joined that company in Apr, 2023. We thought that our troubles were behind us now. But much to our dismay, the company told my son (in Aug) that they wouldn't apply for his work sponsorship (T2 Skilled Worker Visa). The cost is too high at £16,000+ (for five years). My son's boss was urging his bosses to spend the amount and keep him. Not only was my son's work satisfactory to very good, they had earlier spent 6 months looking for someone like him but couldn't get one. It was in limbo for another 5 months. Finally they agreed. They had to raise his salary to £29,900/yr to meet the Visa requirement. My son is now having a T2 Skilled Worker visa. After 5 years he can apply for “Independent Leave to Remain” or ILR status which is equivalent to Permanent Residency. But he barely made it. He got his visa in March 2024. Now getting a work visa in UK is even more difficult. In Apr, 2024, the government has raised the minimum salary qualification for applying a T2 Skilled Visa (all foreigners) to £38,700/yr. Believe me, no employer will pay this much even to a (fresh) PhD student, let alone a post-grad. There could be exceptions but don't count on them (you must have solid qualifications, in highest demand degree, immaculate educational career, top colleges, published a lot of research papers, etc.) None of the foreign students from top colleges such as Imperial College, UCL, Oxbridge top colleges such as Balliol, Kings, etc., are able to find jobs. I am assuming that you wish a UK degree and then continue to work there. If that be the case, it will be near impossible for you. Please go to Germany instead. But there too, students are not getting jobs after getting their degree. So check first. 60 lakhs is a lot of money! Even if you come back with a UK Civil Engineering masters, it may take years to pay off your loan with an India job. In a nutshell, COVID, the furlough scheme in 2020-2021, the huge amount of money relief poured into the already fragile British economy (which is always in recession), the loss of jobs, the BREXIT decision, the Ukraine war, the energy crisis and so many factors have crippled the economy there. The British government thinks that there are too many immigrants. They are doing all they can to discourage it. I have also heard that they may relook at the 2-year post Study visa also and reduce it or even abolish it. This is my sincerest advice to you. Edit/correction: Post-Study Work Visa rule changes: The UK Graduate Post-Study Visa is going to continue as is for now. Students will be eligible to apply for PSW Visa. If granted, under-grads (Bachelor) and Grads (Master) will be allowed to stay up to 2 years till they find a work sponsor while PhD students can get up to 3-years visa. The case of Dependents’ Visa: If you intend to continue to live in the UK after getting a T2 Skilled Visa (or even before), you would ideally want to bring your spouse and family into the UK. But here is the catch. If you are married (with/without children) or intend to marry soon and then to bring your spouse/family to the UK on a dependent visa, there are financial conditions. The current minimum family income (combined income) must be £29,000/yr. This is called a ‘minimum income requirement’. Next April (2025), this will be raised to £38,700/yr. This means that you effectively CANNOT hope to bring your partner into the UK from India. You, the person in the UK, must marry someone who is already in the UK, and has a valid work visa. You cannot hope to bring the spouse to the UK because s/he won't be earning in the UK at the time of the Visa application. For that, s/he has to have a work visa and someone must be willing to sponsor and agree to pay £38,700.

Answer: When it comes to Annual Maintenance Charges, the flat owner owes this amount to the Association of Apartment Owners (AAO) or the Cooperative Housing Society (CHS). The AAO/CHS sends the demand notice to the flat owner. In case the flat is rented out, the CHS can charge up to 10% of AMC as Non-Occupancy Charges (in the case of the AAO, there is no such limit or rule). The entire demand is owed by the flat owner. Now who pays is a matter between the landlord and tenant. Usually, the lease contract will/should mention this. The Society can only nudge the tenant and tell him that the AMC is due from the landlord. My honest opinion is that the landlord should pay this amount. He can, if he likes, include this amount in the rent and increase the rent accordingly. This is fair to the tenant because then he can claim the HRA that he pays out; otherwise, the tenant pays the AMC out of pocket and gets no tax benefit. Some may claim that the landlord will have to pay extra tax on the inflated rent amount. This too is fair because it is the landlord who has to pay the AMC. If there was no real rent the landlord would be paying it from his pocket. The landlord gets a 30% standard deduction on income from house property via rent.

Question: What are the provisions of income tax act under sec.80DD relating to deductions for expenditure on medical treatment, etc., of handicapped dependent?
Answer: The premium paid for mediclaim/health insurance can be claimed under section 80DD. The limit is ₹50,000 or the actual premium (less GST), whichever is less. The actual hospital or medical expense amount cannot be claimed. To make this clear, let me illustrate with example: Case A) Person has no insurance and undergoes a treatment in a hospital. The bill is ₹2 lakhs. The person has to pay ₹2 lakhs out of own pocket. There is no refund or rebate under income tax. Case B) Person has health insurance cover up to ₹1.5 lakhs. S/he undergoes hospitalization. The total bill is ₹2 lakhs out of which consumables cost is ₹4000. The person has to pay ₹46,000+₹4,000 out of own pocket. The rest will be covered by insurance subject to terms and conditions of room-rent cap, ICU cap, etc. Case C) Person has health insurance cover up to ₹5 lakhs. S/he undergoes hospitalization. The total bill is ₹2 lakhs out of which consumables cost is ₹4000. The person has to pay ₹4,000 out of own pocket for the consumables. The rest will be covered by insurance subject to terms and conditions of room-rent cap, ICU cap, etc. Tip: While buying the health insurance please ensure that there is no cap on ambulance charges, ICU rent, room rent, policy is valid across all cities and towns, etc. If not, the insurance cover is adjusted accordingly. Example: Person has a room rent cap of ₹3,000. But s/he is admitted to a room where the rent is ₹4,500. This is 1.5 times more. Now all his bill itemised amounts are reduced by 1.5 times for the cover. For example, if OT charges are ₹9000, the covered amount will be ₹6,000. If the Doctor's charges are ₹15,000, the insurance will pay ₹10,000 and so on. Not only that, for the same treatment, for the same operation, by the same Doctor, the charges are different as per room category. Many hospitals state that only a Deluxe AC room is available and not a standard shared non-AC room. This jacks up the bill. Medical treatment is no longer a holy and pious profession where the only goal is to heal the sick. A note on cross-city policies. Some policies are cheaper because treatment is valid in a Tier-2 or Tier-3 city/town. Treatment in Visavadar is cheaper than the same treatment in Bhavnagar and that in turn is cheaper than in Ahmedabad. So be careful. If for advance treatment, you have to go to these Tier-1 cities, you will find yourself short.

Question: Is a monthly SIP or a lump sum investment profitable?
Answer: There are pros and cons of both methods - SIP vs lumpsum. A lumpsum investment depends upon the timing of investment. Suppose when you invest, the market and consequently the fund NAV is high and later the market tumbles, there will be notional loss. If you panic and sell, there will be a real loss. But over the long term, the market usually rises higher than before than at the time of investment. So in the long term, usually there is a gain. Lumpsum also means higher quantum of investment though even a small one-time investment is also lumpsum. Unfortunately, one cannot time the market and the investment. It is with respect to the timing that the SIP is better. The SIP investment takes this factor out of the equation. The disadvantage is in a constantly rising market. Each SIP is at higher NAV and hence each quantum gain is lesser. The SIP can be as low as ₹500 - some funds are also permitting an SIP of just ₹100. So SIP can be available to anyone. In the greater scheme of things, SIP is recommended for young people who are trying to build wealth and vice versa. But there is no right or wrong for anyone.

Question: Why are the leftists anti-nationals?
Answer: I am a fan of Star Trek, especially the series The Next Generation. There is a very interesting episode in the 7-season series called The Drumhead. This episode is an investigation to find a traitor and it soon becomes like a courtroom drama on the lines of JAG. Synopsis: A conspiracy to espionage is discovered on the starship USS Enterprise (NCC-1701-D). The culprit is soon found but there is another mystery - an explosion in the Engineering section that destroys the hatch of the Warp Core reactor. Some persons are interrogated and suspicion falls on a young cadet. It is later discovered that he falsified his Starfleet application, and named his grandfather as a Vulcan (a species close to humans) when he was really a Romulan (arch-enemy of the Federation). This begins a trial based on mere suspicion, innuendo and fear-mongering. It becomes a drumhead trial. (A drumhead trial was the name for an archaic form of court martial practised on Earth in the 19th century. Its name derives from the eponymous usage of a drum's head as a seat for the presiding judge in an ad-hoc military tribunal. It is also used as a reference to a kangaroo court in its derogatory form. In such a trial, the accused are deemed guilty until proven innocent. The trial marks presenting insinuations as motives, circumstantial evidence as proof, and a mock judge who has already decided upon the verdict.) This long preamble is necessary to explain my point. Yes, I am a rightist by heart and detest leftist sentiment. But calling leftists as traitors is something that I detest even more. Just because someone’s view does not align with yours does not mean that the other person is an enemy. We have become too paranoid and the jury, judge and executioner - all rolled into one. Trivia: The episode The Drumhead is my 8th favourite episode (out of 178). I find the series fascinating because it was so advanced in its time (1987–1994). It showed flatscreen TVs with touch panels, tablets, etc. It successfully explains how faster-than-light travel is possible (hypothetically, of course) without the effects of time dilation (refer to the movie Interstellar) using the concept of warp bubble, warp core and warp drive using high negative energy derived by mixing matter/anti-matter.

Question: What is the longest halt of an Indian train on any station? One of the trains used to stop at Pune 40 minutes in the early 90s.

Most stops/halts have been reduced as follows: All 2 min → 1 Min All 5 min → 2 min All 10 min → mostly 5 min All longer → mostly 10~15 min Some exceptions may be there. This is mainly for crew rotation, loco change, duty roaster handover, refilling water in coaches, general cleaning, restacking the pantry, etc. This has reduced the train travel time quite a lot.

But some train rakes use the Wilhelm-Jacobs bogie design where a bogie is shared between two attached coaches as shown below: In this case, the number of wheels is much less. Question: Why is the Indian Railways not taking action on delayed trains and shortage of compartments in the train? Is it due to the fact that the Indian Railway has a monopoly?
Answer: The above questions are often asked and I have written the answers to all the above questions many times. The answer to each is a technical and logistical challenge. Why are trains delayed? A] Too many trains Why do trains get delayed, and that too very often on Indian Railways? If we exclude (some of) the Rajdhanis, Shatabdis, VB trains, a train running on the dot of the clock is rare. This is especially so for the non-heavyweight class trains - the ordinary mail/express trains. There is an analogy here if we exclude accidents due to derailments, natural causes, etc. Consider road transport. If there are more vehicles on the road, it leads to congestion and traffic jams. The same distance that may be covered in 15 minutes may take more than one hour if there is congestion and jams. On the Indian Railways, the track capacity has not increased but the number of trains has. A train running at normal speed of 100–110 kph must have a minimum 15-minute gap in between for the reason of safety. But on the trunk chord lines (Howrah-Asansol-Dhanbad-Gaya), Mathura-Kanpur Central, Mumbai-Vadodara, Chennai Central-Arkonnam, Chennai-Villupuram and many others), the trains often have a gap of just 5 minutes. This means that trains have to be run at slower speeds. Any delay causes a cascading effect. Case to the point: Kanpur Central Jn sees the arrival and departure of 452 trains daily as follows: 24 Rajdhani Trains 3 Shatabdi Trains 13 Garib Rath Trains 151 Mail/Express Trains 2 AC Express Trains 4 AC SuperFast Trains 11 Passenger Trains 13 MEMU Trains 12 Sampark Kranti Trains 6 Duronto Trains 173 SuperFast Trains 26 Humsafar Trains 2 Tejas Trains 4 Antyodaya Trains 6 Vande Bharat Trains 2 Amrit Bharat Trains Total 452 These are in both directions. So there are about 226 trains each way. Of course not all these are daily trains. But even if we assume that at least 180 trains arrive and depart in one direction (360 trains daily), this means a gap of 8 minutes per train per direction. This is not just unacceptable and dangerous too. B] Ordinary and Premium Trains Not all trains enjoy the same privilege. The Rajdhani Express, for example, enjoys priority. Other trains are made to wait on the loop to let it pass. I remember travelling on the Up Saurashtra Mail to Mumbai. The train got delayed and was made to halt at Udhana Jn for over two hours to let the Mumbai-bound Rajdhani Express pass. The already late Saurashtra Mail was delayed further and instead of reaching Dadar at around 7 AM, it reached at 10 AM. This is not an isolated case - I just narrated a first-hand experience. C] DFC is still not fully operational India (and surrounding nations) is a unique case where passenger and freight traffic use the same tracks. Goods trains are long and slow. If they have to be stopped, they can do so only over a loop line that is long enough to hold them (to let others pass). The need for a separate section/tracks for freight traffic was realised long time back. Shri A B Vajpayee started the Dedicated Freight Corridor (DFC) in 2003–04. The DFC was caught in the policy paralysis and the massive corruption scandals of UPA I/II. Not just the Railways, but even the Defense of the realm was ignored between 2004 and 2014. (That is why I don’t support the INC and the other myopic parties’ coalition.) Even now, 20 years later the DFC is only partially open. Note that the Southern States are not even on the planning board yet. As also, the DFC will not be able to handle the freight traffic of the other lines. Still, it is a welcome step. D] Train Accidents, Mega-blocks, etc. Train accidents usually happen because of a lack of maintenance, especially of the tracks. Consider the example of Kanpur Central above. If there is a train every 5 minutes, how will the tracks be repaired? Track maintenance including overhead catenary repairs requires halting of train services. This means a “Block”. When the block is for a long duration it means a mega block. At this time, one track is closed a a time, maintained and repaired and then the next track. Needless to say, such a mega block will delay the train services. E] Platforms not available This is an offshoot of problem A (too many trains). Many times free platforms are not available and trains are made to wait on the outer signal. Again, going back to the Kanpur Central example. The station handles 360 trains - 180 down, 180 up. All trains halt here. The station has 10 platforms. Platform 10 is a terminus. How will 9 (or 10) platforms handle 360 trains daily? (I have excluded natural factors such as heavy rains, fog, landslides, floods, etc. here.) “Number of coaches” issue Come what may, the number of coaches on trains cannot be increased beyond 22 for a typical LHB rake (24 for old ICF rakes). This is because: Suffice it to say that trains cannot have more than 22 coaches (or 24) and most trains already have these, even the Rajdhanis. Here is a typical Rajdhani: But just suppose for the sake of argument that we do increase the number of coaches. How many can we increase? Make the train length to 30 coaches? More? This will not solve the problem. I will refer to the “fat man, wide pants” scenario. Increasing coaches to accommodate more passengers is like buying stretchy or oversized pants for a fat person - it works for a while till the new girth fills the gaps. What is the solution? It is alright to talk about problems but there have to be solutions. The solution is extra tracks. But even that is a temporary solution. Increasing tracks (or road width) is again like a “Fat man, oversized pants” solution. That does not mean it should not be done. The problem lies with land acquisition and myopic politics. For years now, we, the locals of Pune and Nashik, have been discussing of a semi-highspeed line between Pune and Nashik. But the NCP (both factions) oppose the move because of farmer lands. I understand that the problem is genuine and we cannot adopt a China-like model here. But the Bullet train is being built and whatever the nay-sayers may say, it has shown the art of being possible. Forget the cost, but there is an approach. New tracks can be built - some on the ground, some elevated and some underground. There is money. It is just a matter of will, political will especially. If an 8 to 14-lane highway (Delhi-Meerut) can be built why not new tracks? The solution is to build new tracks and not just parallel to existing tracks as that may not be always feasible. The other solution is to get rid of many through trains and get back to the connecting chain trains. This may mean inconvenience (changeover at the connecting station) and more time (changeover time) but it will mean lesser crowding. Pooled quota and reservation carryover to connecting trains will lessen the pain. For years, I used to travel from Pune to Porbandar having multiple changeovers (Pune-Dadar, Dadar-Kanalus, Kanalus-Porbandar or alternately Pune-Dadar, Dadar-Ahmedabad, Ahmedabad-Porbandar). In Germany, I was travelling from Hanover to Berlin Hbf and there was a changeover at Munich. So this is possible. The biggest reform that IR can do is to eliminate touts on the reservation system. This can be done by one person one reservation at a time. The person should be linked to an Aadhar and Passport only (no DL, voter ID or other IDs.) (Edit: 15-Jun-2024): Based on a comment by Ashish Tiwari, who said that Japanese BTs run in a 5-minute gap or Delhi Metro trains also have a 2–3 minute gap, I am posting this edit. We must first understand the basic difference. Mumbai locals also run with a 2-minute gap. But these trains are EMU-type (much like the VB trains). They also deploy regenerative braking that allows sudden stops (not the older EMU, MEMU & DEMU rakes). For instance, the Shinkansen train units have an earthquake early warning sensing system. In this case, the train uses regenerative braking and can be stopped from top speed (320+ kph) to dead stop within 10 seconds. The tracks can withstand this kind of tremendous strain. I was writing this answer with reference to Indian Railway infrastructure. In India, we do have signal automation known as Automatic Block Signaling. We must understand the “Block”. A block is the distance between two stations but more precisely the distance between the previous station's final signal (outer) and the next station’s outer signal (distant signal). Every station - even the smallest one - has two signals on each side, 4 in all - incoming outer (distant), incoming inner (home), outgoing inner (near the platform aka starter) and outgoing outer (distant). I have somewhat simplified the diagram here and in the diagram below the signals are outer signals. So here goes: I hope that this diagram explains. In the above situation, the minimum gap is 3 stations. In Mumbai’s suburban, the gap is reduced to 2 stations. But as the Mumbai EMU locals can accelerate and decelerate fast, the top speed does not cross 80 kph, this is achievable. For the other Indian long-distance loco-driven trains, the absolute minimum distance is 5–8 km or 6–8 minutes and to be prudent, it must be 10–12 km and at least 10 minutes. Remember that signal automation, while it exists, there is a great deal of other manual manoeuvres. Note that, as claimed by some, there is no shortage of manpower, resources (coaches and locos) or money in the system.

Question: My friend and I share a flat and submitted a joint house rent agreement to the accounts section of the office. Can a given HRA be recovered in this situation?
Answer: Your situation is very common. It is not just starters and freshers who share apartments and rent (to save cost). Sometimes even senior people share apartments when the job takes them to a new city and where they are not inclined to stay long or spend a lot on rent. As per the HRA claim rules, one must submit a rent agreement or rent receipt to claim the HRA tax rebate or exemption. If your HRA is up to Rs 3,000 per month, you can claim HRA without rent receipts. But, you cannot claim HRA without rent receipts when your HRA exceeds Rs 3,000. You can ask your landlord to give you divided rent receipts in case rent exceed ₹3,000 which most likely it will. You should also check whether you will pay less tax under the new tax regime. From all my calculations, I have generally observed that the New Tax Regime is better when: Under the new tax regime, HRA exemption is not allowed but the tax slabs are better spread out enabling lesser tax in spite of no exemptions.

Question: What is the job scenario for international students in the UK? I would like to work for a few years so that I can recover the money that I will be spending on my Master’s. Given the work permit and visa constraints, can an Indian student find a job?
Answer: I think that this is a very old question but the question is very relevant every year. Not only that, the answer is situational and can change every year. This year is 2024. Do you wish to study in UK and then hope to get a job later? Are you contemplating sending your ward to the UK for further studies? If yes, then my one-sentence simple answer is: Please don’t do it; think of an alternative arrangement. The reasons in TLDR answer is: If you don’t wish a long answer please stop now, trust me blindly on the above statements and do as I say: don't send your wards to the UK for higher studies. Now please read the personal experience of my son who went to the UK in Jan 2021 for his Masters. My son completed his B.E. (Mech) and worked for just under 20 months in Pune as a trainee engineer. He appeared for the GRE and his score was 319/340. He also appeared for ToEFL where his score was 115/120. With these scores, he could have secured admission into next-top-25 schools (colleges) in the USA. Well, maybe - never tried anywhere because the Trump administration previously had discouraged H1B visas. My nephew failed to get an H1B twice and continued working on EAD on an H4 visa (fortunately, he has secured the visa now). I thought that I should not take a chance. I prospected Australia, UK and Germany. Finally, I chose UK for the sake of familiarity only. In retrospect, this was an error. We secured his admission to Brunel University London, Uxbridge for his Masters (M.Sc.) in Advanced Engineering Design (he was always inclined in Design). Tuition fees = £17,500 as it was then, hostel fees extra. In Mar 2022, he completed his Masters, scored a distinction, and then we applied for his 2-year Graduate Work Visa (cost = £2800 as it was then). For nearly a year, he could not find any job. There (in the UK at least), there are no campus recruitment drives, no placement service, no real guidance. Students at Masters and above level are expected to find jobs themselves. For over a year, we (him and I) applied to over 250 companies - each time tailoring the CV to suit the job description (as much as we could). We tried a few German companies also. It started from hope (he had brilliant academics) to wait (it will happen soon) to near dejection (it doesn’t look likely now or ever). Meanwhile, his first year of education cost ₹30 lakh (tuition fees, hostel, food, etc.) and the second year living cost was another ₹25 lakh. It looked hopeless and we thought of returning to India by June 2023. Then in Jan 23, he received one interview call. It looked good initially and we thought that he has nearly got the job. But then the bomb dropped - we have decided to pursue with another more suitable candidate. That evening, I had to patiently explain to my son (almost crying), buck him up that these things happen and let us continue to try. Then by the will of the Lord, he received another interview call. They liked the CV and his prior work experience matched their line of work (Fibre Glass body design). They called him to Plymouth for a F2F interview also. In Apr 23, my son started working at last. The salary was not large (£26,500/year), the workplace was Plymouth, but it was better than nothing. He joined. You think the troubles were over. Don’t jump to conclusion yet. In Aug that year (15-Aug in fact), my son was informed that they would be unable to sponsor his Tier-2 Skilled Worker Visa because the cost was too great, the then salary limit was high and the company could not justify the cost. Once again tension (KLPD as we call it). His Study Visa would have expired in Apr 24. We started searching again - this time someone who would sponsor. We now had some UK work experience. But again no joy. Then his employer though that if they let my son go they would have to hunt for a replacement. They were unsuccessful for 6 months before my son joined. So they agreed to sponsor his Visa. My sone has got his T2 Skilled Worker Visa for 5 years valid till Apr 2029. After this (in Apr 29), he can apply for an “Indefinite Leave to Remain (ILR)” status and that will make his status as a Permanent Resident. After another year on ILR, he can apply for British Citizenship. That is another story, another chapter. The point of all this ramble is - my son was somewhat lucky. It is almost guaranteed now that new Student Immigrants will not get a T2 Skilled Visa. This is the real stark reality behind the UK Student dream. This does not end here. A couple in the UK must have a disposable income of £2,200~£2,400 to survive. Prasanna Bhalerao's answer to What is the reality of working in the UK as an Indian immigrant today? Pros and cons ? All in all, it is not a great expense to study in the UK and live there. After studying, there is no guarantee of a job - the UK has been in more or less permanent recession for ages - since 1992 is what I will claim. The salaries are poor. And finally, the new Visa rules have made it nearly impossible for immigrants - not just from India but from all countries outside EU. Check other countries as options - Australia or Germany. But the job situation is Germany is also not good because of the Ukraine war. My best advice will be to look for a career in India.

Then my father got a job at the quarries of Shri Digvijay Cements at a village called Gop Jam (on the railway line of Porbandar to Jamnagar). My mother, sister and I lived in Jamnagar for schooling. In 1971, we (mother, sister and I) moved to Nashik fearing the danger of the 1971 Indo-Pak war and proximity of Jamnagar to Pakistan. In 1972, we moved to Porbandar and did my schooling there.

Question: Is it lucrative to invest in real estate in Chennai? What are some luxury properties worth investing in?
Answer: One must really understand the concept of “investing in real estate”. If a property is purchased for self occupation then it is not an investment in the financial sense. Heck! It is not even to be counted when accounting for net worth. This is because a property used for self-occupation will not be sold, traded, etc., unless one is in the direst of dire financial muddles. Yes, some will sell it but only to buy a better place. Some may also sell to downsize (a popular concept in the US; watch the show Tiny House Nation). A property, be it basic or luxurious, is an investment only if derives an income. The property could be residential or commercial (ignoring Agricultural property here as I don't think this applies in urban area). Now here is my unshakable belief: Luxurious or not, a residential property is not worth investing in, be it Chadani Chowk or Chennai. A residential property doesn't even recover the sunken cost even after 25 years, considering everything. I have written a detailed analytical answer on this. [1]On the other hand, a commercial property can be (?) a better investment. Again it depends and as I don't have the analysis, I can't say for sure. The advantage of a luxurious property is ceremonial and self-gratifying. But it can make a personal difference. Do know that such a property will have much higher maintenance, property tax, etc. But if have the money and can afford it, then you can take an informed decision. Many people (followers of Rich Dad, Poor Dad) equate asset = investment. That is extremely incorrect.

Question: How much will my electricity bill be if I use a 1.5 ton split AC 3 star for 6 hours daily?
Answer: See, the AC is just one appliance in your home that uses electricity. There are others too - lights, fans, TV, fridge, mixer/grinder, microwave, water heater, washing machine, etc. Even the light weight mobile chargers, wifi routers will consume electricity. A TV on standby also uses small electricity. Then there are less used equipment such as irons, etc. Do you have a dishwasher? That will also consume electricity. The electrical billing is as per slabs. It starts at ₹6/unit or so and can jump to as high as ₹20/unit. I mean not actual per unit rate but simple formula of total bill/total units. Next, it totally depends upon the AC usage setting. Finally, You may have multiple ACs in the home and all may be operating from time to time or even simultaneously. Avoid simultaneously use, because then the meter runs faster than Ussain Bolt. So calculating only for a single AC usage is very difficult, nearly impossible. But assuming one AC only, in AUTO mode, a 3-star AC can consume 1.6 to 1.7 units per hour. So that is 10 units per day or 300 units per month. Problem is we cannot assume any specific rate per unit because as explained earlier it will change as per slabs (300-400, 401-500, etc.; don't know the exact slabs). In my home this month, 2 ACs, washing machine twice a week, dishwasher every alternate day, and all other standard appliances, lights jacked up the usage to 492 units - up from 255 the previous month. The bill for April,2024 was ₹7052 - it was ₹3190 for March, 2024. Had the units crossed 500, I would have been in the next slab and bill could have been more than ₹8000 (my guess). This is as per billing rates in Pune, Maharashtra.

Question: When should one exit MF or at least book profits given that the investment is of more than 10 years and portfolio is in lakhs?
Answer: There is no one right or wrong way. There are so many factors: Are you in need of the funds or simply think “enough is enough”? Remember that “booking profit” cannot be the sole motive. Let us say you redeem and book the profit. There can be a substantial LTCG to pay but let us assume that you know that and are ready to pay that also. The question is what next? I mean what will you do with the money? If that money is going to be used for some purpose or expense, then it is fine. Whether that purpose or expense is right or wrong is not for me or anyone to decide. You have thought about it and you decided to go ahead. Then it is fine. Go ahead, redeem and book your profits. A paper profit is no good, is it? Use your money. What else is the purpose of money? Just remember to spend well. If that money is simply going to be reinvested again - maybe after some time? Then what is the point of booking the profits if the fund is performing well? You would lose on LTCG and you will be locked in another fund for at least a year (to avoid exit load). Are you expecting the market to fall and you will book high profits now and reinvest when the bears grip the market? That would be very unwise because one cannot time the market and one should not even attempt to do it. Sure, one can get lucky once in a while but it is a risky game.

Question: Is there a pension revision in NPS? Does the pension increase with time?
Answer: Unlike OPS where Pension is decided as per the respective pay commissions’ recommendations, NPS is market-driven. At the time of superannuation (retirement), the subscriber has the option to encash up to 60% of the corpus (to be invested as the person likes) while the balance amount is used to buy an annuity policy that pays pension. The pension amount of the annuity is more or less fixed for life. One may ask, how will ₹20,000/mo (or whatever) paid at the start will suffice after 5, 10, 15, 20 years if it remains the same? The answer is the balance 60% that one has at one’s disposal. Invest it wisely in Balanced or Hybrid Mutual Funds and one can get an 8–9% return on equity. Set up an SWP. Assuming that the monthly requirement is ₹50,000/mo at the start (over and above the pension payout), the inflation rate is uniform 6%, then a corpus sum of ₹1.4 Cr is sufficient to last till the age of 100. Where to get ₹1.4 Cr? This can be 60% of the NPS fund, PF, PPF, savings in banks, money invested in capital markets, etc. Note that ₹50,000 (plus ₹20,000) is for basic living only and does not cater for any big-ticket expenses such as foreign holidays, home renovations/maintenance, new car/appliances, higher education and marriage expenses of children, etc. Remarks: 1. All corpus invested in Balance Advantage type funds (Equity oriented) where LTCG tax = 10% after one year. 2. LTCG is paid on the actual gain on the actual SWP amount (redemption) every year.

Question: If you pay property taxes, who actually owns your land?
Answer: In India … There are a few types of properties in India: a) Built on freehold land that was purchased by the owner and later s/he built a property on it. This kind of property belongs to the owner in totality. But see the next two points. b) Built on land that was/is part of a Resident Welfare Association (RWA). It was purchased by the owner and later s/he built a property on it. This kind of property belongs to the RWA and the owner owns a share of the base land in proportion to his property. But see the next point. c) A property or land or apartment/building is part of a Cooperative Housing Society (CHS). Usually, a CHS is formed for a block of flats in one or many buildings situated on a plot of land. But sometimes a CHS could also be formed to own independent houses, rowhouses, townhouses, etc. In all these cases the property - the land, the buildings, the flats/houses, the equipment/assets belong to the CHS. The buyer is a member of the CHS and has more or less permanent residency rights. d) Properties built on leasehold plots on a 99-year or 999-year lease. Needless to say, that plot/land is leased and the original owner retains the right to the land. There could be some other examples but the above are major ones. Who pays the tax does not determine the ownership. In many cases, properties are let out and (unscrupulous) landlords make the tenants pay the property tax. Does this mean that ownership transfers to the tenants? Having clarified the issue of ownership, let me explain what happens if one fails to pay the property tax in time: In all types of ownership, the individual who occupies the dwelling receives a tax demand. If the demand is not paid in time, a fine and interest is levied. When the outstanding amount becomes too high, it becomes a court case for recovery proceedings. The owner/occupier may be evicted from the dwelling. The property can be sold/auctioned off. The owner/occupier can be jailed. In case of a CHS, the CHS is also sent the notice to action. The society can cancel the membership of the member and force evacuate the premises.

Question: What are the advantages of a 5-star inverter split AC?
Answer: As per my own strict opinion only … A 5-star AC is overrated and over advertised as a device that will save one huge amount of money over time. This is true in one way but no one (manufacturer) will ever tell you the real facts and the story. I was always sure that I did not need a 5-star AC, being residing on the first floor, not exposed to the Westerly Sun, etc. But I still did a comparison. I used a Panasonic 1.5 ton AC for this exercise, but you can use any popular brand. My comparison may surprise you. Let me assume that the per unit charge is ₹8. Let me keep the annual usage hours the same (4.38 hr/day). So the 5-star AC would cost us ₹6,200 per year whereas the 3-star unit would deplete our bank by ₹ 7,784/yr. This is a saving of ₹ 1,584/yr. The upfront cost difference is ₹9,000. Not even accounting for interest loss on this amount, it will take 6 years to recover the cost. My next analysis was based on real usage. To me, a resident of Pune, it was a no brainer - we use the AC from 15-Mar to 15-Jun and then again in 15-Oct to 15-Nov - or 4 months a year. The running time during this time is about 5 hours (for the maximum used AC in the home) or 600 hours/yr (5 x 4 x 30). But let me assume Delhi or any city in hot Central India where the AC may run up to 7 hours (maximum used AC) and for 7 months a year (Mar to Jul and Sep-Oct). That becomes 1470 units a year or let me even out to 1500 unit/yr. This would mean that the 5-star AC will become cheaper to operate after 6 years and 1 month. (By my usage statistics, my 3-star AC costs an extra ₹ 592 to run per year and it will be 15 years and 2 months before I recover the cost.) My final question is how long do people keep the AC before replacing? Modern electronics are prone to frequent failures. My Hitachi 1.5T Window AC with bare minimum of any electronics worked from 2001 to 2023. It was still in excellent working condition and I replaced it only because I renovated my home (and also because it was very noisy). These things don’t happen now. You may replace your AC in 8 years or 10 years - up to you - but you are very likely to replace it. So, my opinion says that unless one uses an AC for 12+ hours a day, for all 12 months a year (like in an office), there is no point of buying a 5-star rated AC. (I have a lurking suspicion that in an office where near constant cooling is required, where the compressor may work all the time, a non-inverter, cheaper AC may be a better option. But then I don’t like to speak or opine without data.)

Question: My gold got auctioned off from a Muthoot gold loan. How do I get that gold back?
Answer: This is most unfortunate. Pledged gold is auctioned off as the last resort when all avenues to recover the loan against gold (principal + interest + penalties) is not possible. Question: What are the top recommendations for 1.5-ton non-inverter split ACs?
Answer: How very interesting! Member Karthik asked me a very similar question yesterday. His AC had broken down and he was looking to replace the AC in his 140 sq foot room. But first a note to the OP: Buying an AC is not as simple as it sounds. The room size is just, and just one, of the many parameters. I will attempt to explain. There are many factors. A] ROOM SIZE, TYPE, PEOPLE => TONNAGE? A 1 Ton AC can suffice a room between 110 sqft to 125 sqft easily. It can also work for your 140 sqft room, if your room is on the lower floor and not directly hit by the sun and your usage is less than 4 hours a day, < 5 months a year, a 1 T AC would suffice. The general rule of thumb is: But do consider the Sun factor and room exposure to the Sun. B] IS YOUR AC REALLY A 1-TON OR 1.5-TON, ETC.? The first thing is to disbelieve whatever you are told. A 1T AC is not really a 1T AC (it may be 0.86T), a 1.5T AC is not really a 1.5T AC (it may be 1.33T) and so on. Check the normal BTU (British Thermal Units) of the AC. The real AC Tonnage is: BTU / 12000 = Real AC Tonnage If that is the case, why and how do manufacturers get away with these blatantly false claims? This is because modern inverter AC has multimode operation options (5-in-1, 6-in-1, 7-in-1), etc. One of the modes is High Cool mode where AC runs at 110-120% capacity. So a 0.86T AC is passed off as 1T, 1.33T at 110% = 1.463 T and so on. But obviously, if the real requirement is high cooling then such a lower-powered AC is going to work extra to cool and your power bill will increase. So the first rule - check the BTU of the AC and calculate the real tonnage. Most Samsung ACs do not mention or release BTU specs for this reason. That is why I don't trust them not that they are bad. C] 3-STAR OR 4-STAR OR 5-STAR? Next to decide is whether to go for 3-star or 5-star. Avoid 1-star and 2-star AC. If your running is less than 10 hours per day and limited to 6 months or less a year, then there is no need for a 5-star AC. A 3-Star is good enough. If there are still doubts about usage then a 4-star can be considered. On the other hand, a 5-star AC at a higher upfront cost will work out cheaper in the long-running operations (daily or yearly). D] MULTI-MODE OPERATION (5-IN-1, 6-IN-1, 7-IN-1, ETC.) AND OTHER FEATURES These features can be useful though in most case people do not use them. Multi-mode operation allows the AC to be used in multiple capacities - High Cool (110%+), Fast Cool (100%), 90%, 60%, 40%, etc. There is AUTO cool also that decided everything - manufacturers are calling this AI and/or Smart AC though there is nothing rocket science about it. Most people use AC in AUTO mode. Horizontal Swing or 4-way swing. Vertical swing or 2-way is always there. But 4-way swing is a feature that is available on higher-end models only. 95% of 3-star and lower AC models won’t have it. 4WS cools the room more uniformly and is useful if the AC indoor unit placing is slightly askew. WiFi, and Alexa/Google are something nice to have but not strictly necessary. If the cost jumps up because of these, please avoid such a unit. I would say, up to ₹1000 extra is OK. Not a penny more. But such ACs do have a Smartphone App (Android and iOS) and do help in simple diagnosis. E] OUTDOOR UNIT INSTALLATION The placement of the outdoor compressor unit also matters. You should place it so that it is not on the roof or exposed to direct afternoon sun (morning is OK). North, North-East, and East are OK - other directions are not and the roof should be avoided. If the roof installation cannot be avoided, consider putting up a tiny shed over the unit. If outdoor units receive heat from the sun directly, their efficiency goes down. F] INSTALLATION COSTS Now, this is one area where costs are standardised somewhat. These are payable over and above. But the manufacturer mentions the standard installation cost only - like ₹1200 + GST. The AC comes with a 3-meter copper tube and drain pipe only. Extra copper pipe is about ₹275/ft. This is usually insufficient. Cost of outdoor unit stand - this is about ₹850 extra. Core cutting charges are extra - these are ₹130/inch. Expect the total installation cost between ₹3500 to ₹5000. AC unit core-cutting in progress G] CHECK THE WARRANTY Before buying check the warranty. There are a few ACs like Voltas that do not offer any warranty or less warranty on the PCB. Please consider what warranty is offered on the Compressor, PCB and full unit - it should be a minimum 10, 5 and 1 respectively. Extended warranty? This is your call. But an extended warranty is on the whole unit and may cover 2, 3 or 4 years. Usually, and my experience says, nothing really significant happens during this time. As also, the warranty - regular or extended - does not cover misuse, electrical supply problems (next point), etc. I did not purchase the extended warranty. In fact, one of my 4 ACs is an old 1-ton Sansung unit of 2006 and nothing has happened to it except that I had to recharge/refill the gas once. H] STABILIZER-FREE OPERATION Again do not believe the manufacturer’s claim that no stabilizer is required. I highly recommend it. If your AC is going to run for more than 5 hours or there is fluctuation in your area, buy a stabilizer. If your AC PCB is damaged due to voltage fluctuation, the warranty is voided. A new PCB is at least ₹8000 but could be more also. A stabilizer - costing ₹2000 or so - from a reputed brand brings peace to the mind. Better safe than sorry. (I have 4 AC in my home but I have not purchased a separate stabilizer for each AC This is because I have a 32A 3-phase stabilizer at the mains. And yet, for the fridge, I have purchased a stabilizer from v-guard.) BRAND … BRAND … BRAND … Finally, the brand. I AM NOT RECOMMENDING ANY BRAND JUST LISTING MY RESEARCH DETAILS. Recently, I purchased 2 new 1.5T 3-star ACs for my home (one more is an existing Samsung unit). All were Panasonic. I arrived at the decision after a detailed study: I studied all the brands and concluded that LG, Panasonic, Daikin and Carrier are the best. Others are less powerful, too noisy, not enough warranty (like Voltas), etc. This is as of 2023–24. This may change every year. Once again my opinion. Just to make it clear Some Tips: Hope this essay helps all.

Question: What are some smart ways to reduce unnecessary expenses and increase savings without drastically changing one's lifestyle?
Answer: This is my own saying (I invented it) … If you don't know what you are doing, you don't know what you are doing wrong. Applying this saying here, if you don't know what you are spending, and where your money is going, you won't know whether that spending is useful or wasteful. So if you wish to save money and cut down on wasteful spending, the very first thing to do is keep a record. Write down or log each and every paisa/penny/cent you spend. Every day, you should make a note of what was your ending balance the previous day, what were your expenditures on that day and what was the ending balance that day. Everything, repeat everything, should be tallied. Best to do this in a spreadsheet. You must be as granular as possible. For example, if you go to the market, while you need not classify and record each and every item, you must not club at the same time. For example, you can record as vegetables, groceries, household items, etc. If you are shopping online, don't record it as one single online transaction with a consolidated bill. Spread it to a fair degree on categories of items. Once, you start recording, tag each spending as “absolutely essential”, “somewhat required”, “avoidable”, “extravagant”, etc. You can add more classes but don’t go beyond 5. You can be your judge as what classifies as what but very practical and pragmatic about it. If you are competent with Excel, create various pivot charts. Now you can know what you are doing wrong. Question: I have done my 3rd to 10th from Saudia Arabia. and 11th, 12th I have done from India. will I fall under NRI category?
Answer: NRI or Non Resident Indian is a certificate of tax filing status. If an Indian citizen is resident outside India for more than 182 days (total stay and not necessarily contiguous), then his/her income outside India for that financial year is not taxed. The NRI status may change every year depending upon the above clause. NRI is not a citizenship and in fact doesn't apply to foreigners, PIOs, OCIs, etc. If the person is an NRI and had some income in India, then that income is taxable in India. Answer: All companies in India are required to follow PF laws. The minimum PF contribution that the employer must contribute is 8% and maximum is 12%. You can instruct the company to deduct more than ₹7,800 and the amount over this amount is known as VPF or Voluntary PF. But your employer will contribute only that much that is stipulated by law (₹7,800/mo or 12%) and not more. Note that the employees today have the option to opt out if the PF scheme. In this case, the employer must pay the employee the promised PF amount as stated in the CTC breakup into gentler salary. This means more disposable income but not only the additional income is taxed, you lose the tax rebate as well as saving for your retirement corpus.

Question: Is the bank FD interest TDS deducted per bank or all banks of the same person with the same PAN?
Answer: Let us assume that you have a term deposit in Bank A. This bank will deduct TDS as per rules if Form 15G/15H is not submitted. If you open fixed deposits in different branches and in different banks, each bank/branch will deduct TDS as per the information it holds. That is, it does not know about other FDs that you hold elsewhere. To explain this with an example, if you invest ₹ 2,00,000 and the interest rate is 7%, you will get an interest income of ₹ 14,000. Since this figure exceeds ₹ 10,000 your bank will deduct TDS on it. However, if you divide this FD between 3 different banks, you will get an interest of ₹ 4,666.67 in each bank. Since each amount is below the threshold of Rs. 10,000 the banks will not deduct TDS on the same. That is as far as your question is concerned. But ultimately all information on other income such as Bank Savings account interest, Bank FD interest, share capital dividend, income from various SSS instruments held in banks/Post Office, short-term or long-term capital gains due to sale of fixed/liquid assets, etc., all is reported to the Income Tax department. It appears in the 26AS statement. When you file the returns, the income from these sources is automatically linked and added to the return. So you will have to pay tax. Secondly, we must pay advance tax when TDS is not automatic. Just for example, if you had interest of ₹4,666.67 from three FDs in three banks (and nothing else), it is still your moral duty to deposit advance tax (self-assessment) because banks could not deduct these.
