Question: If I invest Rs. 2000000 in the stock market, roughly how much can I earn per month?
Answer: When you invest in stocks, the companies where you invest declare dividends from time to time. These are the only earnings. Dividends are usually annual and in some cases, semi-annual. There are no monthly earnings. The Dividend is a fixed amount per share held. It is not guaranteed though you can look at history, current declared profits (EBDITA), etc., and guess. The monthly amount can be determined by dividing the total dividend received divided by 12. Note that the dividend is subject to income tax. If you mean how much can I expect to earn by stock market investment - other than dividend - then it is ZERO. Stocks rise and fall. What you hold in your current portfolio is unrealised gain or unrealised loss. It is converted to real gain/loss when you sell. Some of the following are deductible fees based on the broker: - Brokerage and GST on Brokerage - Securities Transaction Tax (STT) - Exchange Fees levied by the exchange (NSE or BSE) + GST - SEBI Fees - Stamp Duty (These are approximately 0.1% to 0.7% of the total traded value and payable at the time of buying as well as selling) Stock market (real) gains/losses are not predictable. Both can be very high, medium, or near zero. If you are looking at guaranteed income, you should stick to Fixed Maturity Plans such as Bank Term Deposits (FD), various Small Saving Schemes, etc.

Question: Is it better to pay capital gains tax on sale of immovable property in India than investing in purchase of a second house & keeping it vacant for three years?
Answer: No. Investing in a second property - whatever may be the reason - from earning secondary/passive income via rent or investing now to sell later (at a profit) or to save tax on an old property sale - any reason whatsoever is not a good idea. The only property type worth investing in is a Commercial Property. But: The I-T Act lets you save long-term capital gains on property if you invest the entire gain in a residential property or capital gains bonds. These investments have to be made either within a year before the sale of the property, or within two years of the transaction. Source: How to save tax on long-term capital gains on property - Want to save long-term capital gains? Return on capital invested in a residential property are very low. Many people quote that some people purchased a property somewhere for ₹4 lakhs in 1985 and sold it for ₹3 Cr today. These are absolute returns and not realistic. Calculate the CAGR and the return is a mere 11% (or less). This does not take into account the cost of maintenance, refurbishing, property tax, society fees paid, etc. Besides, try selling a nearly 40-year-old property today for any sum - unless there is a redevelopment scheme. If there is proposed redevelopment, the owner wants to enjoy the fruits. Residential property is not only a poor investment, it is 99% of the time a dead investment. The benefit of a property is when it is used as leverage for a loan or such. My advice: After selling the property, invest up to ₹50 lakhs in Capital Gains Bonds that will offset that much from the CG under Section 54ec. Capital Gains Bonds come with a lock-in period of five years from the date of issuance. They earn a taxable interest at 5.25% per annum. After 5 years, surrender the bonds. Pay Capital Gains on the balance amount. Your money will lose value because of inflation (about ₹11 lakhs at 6%) but it is liquid all the same. On this ₹50 lakhs invested in Bonds, you would have saved an LTCG tax of ₹9,88,000. So it is not a bad deal.

All persons born in India between 26 January 1950 and 1 July 1987 automatically received citizenship by birth regardless of the nationalities of their parents. Between 1 July 1987 and 3 December 2004, citizenship by birth was granted if at least one parent was a citizen. Individuals born in the country since then receive Indian citizenship at birth only if both parents are Indian citizens, or if one parent is a citizen and the other is not considered an illegal migrant. Foreigners may become Indian citizens by naturalisation after residing in the country for at least 12 years and renouncing any previous nationalities. Members of certain religious minority communities from neighbouring countries qualify for a reduced residence requirement of six years. Indian citizens who permanently settle in Pakistan or Bangladesh, or voluntarily acquire foreign citizenship automatically lose Indian citizenship. Dual citizenship is allowed in certain cases of minor children. Source: Indian nationality law - Wikipedia

Question: How do I recover society maintenance dues from a member who is not paying?
Answer: The secretary of the Society must send notices and reminders to the defaulting member. The following must be explained in the letter: See below: Expulsion of a Member in a Co-operative Housing Society is an extreme measure and most Societies consider it their last resort. When everything else fails to set things right, the expulsion of the concerned Member is considered the only way out. If the extreme need arises for the expulsion of a Member, the Law and Procedure be strictly followed as laid down in Section 35 of Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act 1960, Rules 28, 29 of the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Rule 1961 read with Bye-laws No.51 to 56 of Model Bye-laws. Grounds of Expulsion of a Member: A Member may be expelled from the Membership of the Society if such a Member: A Society may, by Resolution passed [by a majority of not less than three-fourths] of the Members entitled to vote who are present at a General Body Meeting held for the purpose, expel a Member for acts ‘which are detrimental to the interest or proper working of the Society’. No Resolution shall be valid, unless the Member concerned is given an opportunity of representing his case to the General Body and no Resolution shall be effective unless it is approved by the Registrar. Effect of Expulsion on Membership of the Society:- The Member, duly expelled from Membership of the Society, shall cease to be the Member of the Society, with effect from the date on which the Resolution of expulsion from the Membership of the Society is approved by the Registrar of Co-op. Societies. Handing Over of Flat: The Member who has been duly expelled from the Membership of the Society, shall not be entitled to continue in occupation of his flat and he shall arrange to hand over peaceful and vacant possession of his flat to the Secretary of the Society within such period as the Managing Committee may allow. On his failure to do so, he shall be liable to be evicted from his flat. Readmission to Membership:- No Member of the Society, who has been expelled from the membership, shall be eligible for readmission to membership in the Society, until the expiry of the period of one year from the date of his expulsion, provided that on the recommendation of the General Body of the Society, the expelled Member may be readmitted to its membership, as a special case before the expiry of the period of one year with the prior permission of the Registrar of Co-operative Societies. Considering that the basic duty of a Cooperative Housing Society Member is to safeguard the interests of the Society any Member whose actions are detrimental to the interests of the Society can be expelled. The process of expulsion is a fair one, where both parties i.e. the Managing Committee and the Member likely to be affected, are given an opportunity to express their points of view. If the Managing Committee of a Cooperative Housing Society decides to expel a Member from the membership of the Society, a Resolution needs to be passed to that effect; the topic must be included in the Agenda of the next General Meeting. The Member who is likely to be affected must be given a minimum one-month notice to remain present at the General Meeting or then make a written submission to Show-Cause why he should not be expelled. Only then can the General Body proceed to consider the Resolution for expulsion of the Member. This Resolution, however, needs to be supported by not less than 3/4 of the Members entitled to vote and present at the General Meeting and once the Resolution is passed, it needs to be forwarded to the Registering Authority for approval. Question: Why are salaries taxed if corporate tax is already paid by companies?
Answer: Income tax is just as it implies - a tax on income. Corporate tax is tax on company’s gross profit or company’s income. It is tax on the operating earnings of a company after deducting costs from the cost of the goods sold (COGS) and income depreciation. Personal income tax is tax on person’s income. It has nothing to do with the company’s income. That, that company has paid corporate tax and therefore employee salary should not be taxed is flawed argument. As explained above corporate tax is paid after deducting company’s costs which includes salaries and expenses on employees. Tomorrow, one may argue - the CEO has paid the tax so I, a lower wrung employee shouldn’t pay tax. This is just as ridiculous an argument.

Question: Why can’t Indian Railways refund 50% of the amount to RAC passengers if they don't get full berth until their destination?
Answer: I will explain the typical sleeper class (non AC) charges. More or less same applies to other classes. The breakup is: Base Fare + Reservation Charges + Superfast Charges + GST = Total Fare. In other classes, there is also Dynamic Fare (before GST). Earlier, there used to a component called sleeper berth charges (free for children below 12 years). This is now subsumed elsewhere. So now, it is promised that those with confirmed reservation will get a sleeper berth. While it does seem unfair that people with RAC ticket are also charges the full fare, note that fare cannot be reduced to 50% or something like that. In fact, as the railways gives a huge subsidy on 2nd class tickets, any further subsidy or reduction cannot be given. Not just that, RAC passengers can get a confirmed berth enroute. So the onus of collecting the fare lies with the TTE. We all know how effeciately, smoothly and transparently a person dependant fare collection system works in the Railways. The other issue will be fight leading to fare calculation. Let us say, a person is travelling from Mumbai to New Delhi. He hold an RAC ticket. When the train reaches Ratlam, he gets a berth against cancellation. Should the balance fare be between Ratlam and New Delhi? If yes, why? He has been travelling on train since the origin. If not, why not? He got the berth from Ratlam. So, it does not solve problems and instead leaves considerable patronage in the hands of the TTE. The passenger knows that s/he is getting an RAC ticket. S/he knows very well that the whole journey may be spent sitting on the side lower berth. Yet s/he chose to book it because s/he is of the opinion that travel is more important than comfort. So the person cannot complain now. My personal view: The RAC system is flawed and should be abolished. Everybody gets either a confirmed berth or is on waiting list. There is no concept of RAC on daytime sitting-only trains anyway. Waiting list should be limited to 30 berths per coach (per 78 berths) If and when there are cancellations, the WL advances just like now. This way all passengers with confirmed reservation can travel with the same comfort as the other passengers in that same coach.
